_comment: Debate modes are interchangeable PROTOCOLS. Each `phases` object maps a phase name to the per-turn instruction given to an agent when the engine is in that phase. R/debate_engine.R::select_phase() maps a round number to a phase name using this ladder: round 1 -> 'opening'; final round -> 'closing'; the round before the final -> 'revision' (if present) else 'reflection' (if present); all other rounds alternate 'response' and 'cross_examination'. Any phase the engine asks for but a mode omits falls back to 'response', then 'opening'. Add a mode by adding an object here -- no R changes.

debate_modes.name: Oxford
debate_modes.description: Two sides argue a motion; structured rebuttal.

phases.opening: State your side's position on the motion clearly, with your two strongest supporting arguments.
phases.response: Rebut the previous speaker's strongest point directly, then advance a new argument for your side.
phases.cross_examination: Ask one pointed question exposing a weakness in the opposing side, then answer the strongest question posed to you.
phases.revision: Concede any point the debate has genuinely won against you, and sharpen the argument you are most confident in.
phases.closing: Deliver a closing statement: summarize why your side should prevail on the balance of arguments.

phases.opening: Give your independent estimate/position on the question, with brief justification. Do not reference other participants.
phases.response: Having seen the range of positions, state whether and why you are revising your own. Move toward or away from the group as the arguments warrant.
phases.reflection: Identify the remaining source of divergence in the group and what evidence would resolve it.
phases.closing: Give your final position and your confidence in it.

debate_modes.name: Courtroom
debate_modes.description: Prosecution, defense, and a weighing of evidence.

phases.opening: Present your opening argument as prosecution or defense of the proposition, previewing your evidence.
phases.response: Examine the evidence just presented: what does it prove, what does it not, and what is missing?
phases.cross_examination: Cross-examine the opposing argument: expose assumptions, gaps, and admissibility problems.
phases.closing: Deliver your closing argument to the finder of fact.

phases.opening: Present a clear, falsifiable hypothesis relevant to the topic, with the mechanism you propose.
phases.response: Critically review the most recent hypothesis: strengths, flaws, confounders, and missing controls.
phases.reflection: Assess the statistical/evidentiary basis of the round's claims and flag weak inference.
phases.closing: Synthesize: what is well-supported, what needs more study, and the strongest hypothesis standing.

phases.opening: State the claim under review and the criteria by which it should be judged.
phases.response: Review against the criteria: major concerns, minor concerns, and what would need to change to accept it.
phases.revision: Propose the specific revisions that would address the concerns raised.
phases.closing: Give a recommendation: accept, minor revision, major revision, or reject, with reasons.

phases.opening: Ask probing questions only. Do NOT propose answers yet -- surface the hidden assumptions in the topic.
phases.response: Ask a follow-up question that presses on the weakest assumption exposed so far.
phases.reflection: Name the assumptions the questioning has revealed and which now look untenable.
phases.closing: Now answer the strongest open questions, citing which question you are answering.

phases.opening: Give your expert perspective on the topic in your own domain's terms.
phases.response: Respond to a point another panelist made, agreeing or disagreeing with reasons.
phases.closing: Give your final takeaway for the audience.

phases.opening: Contribute your opening view on the topic.
phases.response: Build on or challenge the discussion so far, adding something new.

phases.opening: Voice your stakeholder group's central concern or hope regarding the topic.
phases.response: React to another stakeholder's concern: where do your interests align or conflict?
phases.closing: State what outcome would best serve the people you represent.

phases.opening: Advance a position on the topic that you will then have to defend against attack.
phases.response: Attack the strongest standing claim as hard as you honestly can, then defend your own.
phases.revision: Repair your position against the attacks that landed, or abandon it if it cannot be repaired.
phases.closing: State what survived the adversarial process.

debate_modes.name: Fishbowl
debate_modes.description: A few speak while others observe, then swap.

phases.opening: As an inner-circle speaker, open the discussion on the topic.
phases.response: Respond to the inner-circle exchange, advancing the conversation.
phases.reflection: As an observer stepping in, reflect on what the inner circle missed.

phases.opening: Contribute your must-have requirement for any acceptable outcome.
phases.response: Identify which requirements are compatible and where the real tensions lie.
phases.revision: Propose a synthesis that satisfies as many must-haves as possible.
phases.closing: State whether you can endorse the emerging synthesis and any reservation you hold.

debate_modes.name: Policy Hearing
debate_modes.description: Testimony and questioning on a proposal.

phases.opening: Give testimony on the proposal from your expertise: expected effects and tradeoffs.
phases.response: Question the previous testimony on feasibility, cost, or unintended consequences.
phases.revision: Recommend amendments that would improve the proposal.
phases.closing: State your final recommendation to the committee.
